fields.subject: index_patient
fields.name: Sanger sequencing of SERPINC1
fields.finding: Compound heterozygous c.235C>T/p.Arg79Cys (mother) and c.1277C>T/p.Ser426Leu (father), both reported pathogenic

evidence.quote: A 10-year-old boy presented to the emergency room with severe left flank pain. He had been diagnosed with a solitary left kidney and IVC agenesis at 4 months of age and has had superficial abdominal varices since birth. At 9 years of age, clinical findings and imaging studies led to the suspicion of KILT syndrome. At that time, laboratory evaluation showed reduced ATIII activity at 56% to 60% (normal range, 82% to 126%). Sanger sequencing confirmed the diagnosis of ATIII deficiency, based on the identification of the following compound heterozygous variants in the SERPINC1 gene: c.235C>T, p.Arg79Cys from his mother, pathogenic [] and c.1277C>T, p.Ser426Leu from his father, pathogenic []. At the emergency department, abdominal computed tomography revealed a left perirenal hematoma (Fig. 1) with renal infarction. His kidney function was within normal range, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 92.26 mL/min/1.73 m2 (calculated using the creatinine-based bedside Schwartz equation) without proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.08 mg/mg) nor hematuria. The patient was admitted to the hospital. He underwent percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD), which initially obtained approximately 3 L of fluid daily, in combination with anticoagulation therapy with warfarin and enoxaparin and ATIII supplementation. Contrary to our expectation, the drainage volume did not decrease, and its character changed from bloody to straw colored with slight turbidity. The drained fluid was predominantly composed of lymphocytes (76%) with 3% polymorphonuclear cells, and biochemical analysis revealed urea nitrogen of 13 mg/dL, creatinine of 0.27 mg/dL, triglyceride <7 mg/dL, glucose 99 mg/dL, protein 0.1 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 33 U/L. These findings were consistent with non-chylous lymphatic leakage. Magnetic resonance lymphangiography demonstrated abnormal venous pressure in the renal hilum, which led to lymphatic fluid accumulation between the renal fascia and renal capsule (Fig. 2). Over time, the initial hemorrhage was absorbed, creating an abnormal space that allowed lymphatic fluid accumulation and persistent perirenal lymphatic effusion. Ethanol sclerotherapy was performed. The drainage volume remained unchanged after the first session but significantly decreased after a total of four sessions over a month. Follow-up imaging clearly showed a decrease in fluid collection, and his symptoms improved. The percutaneous drain was subsequently removed, and the patient was discharged. On outpatient follow-up at 6 months after discharge, the boy remained stable on warfarin without evidence of thromboembolism or hemorrhage. His kidney function was stable, with an eGFR of 81.1 mL/min/1.73 m2 without proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.09 mg/mg). Comparison of kidney ultrasound 18 months before showed less prominent left kidney enlargement from 14.3 cm to 13.1 cm, without evidence of perirenal fluid.

facts.notes: Diagnostic test execution represented alongside existing results; no additional unique finding. Unknown follow-up modality/timing not filled from another visit.

A 10-year-old boy presented to the emergency room with severe left flank pain. He had been diagnosed with a solitary left kidney and IVC agenesis at 4 months of age and has had superficial abdominal varices since birth. At 9 years of age, clinical findings and imaging studies led to the suspicion of KILT syndrome. At that time, laboratory evaluation showed reduced ATIII activity at 56% to 60% (normal range, 82% to 126%). Sanger sequencing confirmed the diagnosis of ATIII deficiency, based on the identification of the following compound heterozygous variants in the SERPINC1 gene: c.235C>T, p.Arg79Cys from his mother, pathogenic [] and c.1277C>T, p.Ser426Leu from his father, pathogenic []. At the emergency department, abdominal computed tomography revealed a left perirenal hematoma (Fig. 1) with renal infarction. His kidney function was within normal range, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 92.26 mL/min/1.73 m2 (calculated using the creatinine-based bedside Schwartz equation) without proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.08 mg/mg) nor hematuria. The patient was admitted to the hospital. He underwent percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD), which initially obtained approximately 3 L of fluid daily, in combination with anticoagulation therapy with warfarin and enoxaparin and ATIII supplementation. Contrary to our expectation, the drainage volume did not decrease, and its character changed from bloody to straw colored with slight turbidity. The drained fluid was predominantly composed of lymphocytes (76%) with 3% polymorphonuclear cells, and biochemical analysis revealed urea nitrogen of 13 mg/dL, creatinine of 0.27 mg/dL, triglyceride <7 mg/dL, glucose 99 mg/dL, protein 0.1 g/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 33 U/L. These findings were consistent with non-chylous lymphatic leakage. Magnetic resonance lymphangiography demonstrated abnormal venous pressure in the renal hilum, which led to lymphatic fluid accumulation between the renal fascia and renal capsule (Fig. 2). Over time, the initial hemorrhage was absorbed, creating an abnormal space that allowed lymphatic fluid accumulation and persistent perirenal lymphatic effusion. Ethanol sclerotherapy was performed. The drainage volume remained unchanged after the first session but significantly decreased after a total of four sessions over a month. Follow-up imaging clearly showed a decrease in fluid collection, and his symptoms improved. The percutaneous drain was subsequently removed, and the patient was discharged. On outpatient follow-up at 6 months after discharge, the boy remained stable on warfarin without evidence of thromboembolism or hemorrhage. His kidney function was stable, with an eGFR of 81.1 mL/min/1.73 m2 without proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.09 mg/mg). Comparison of kidney ultrasound 18 months before showed less prominent left kidney enlargement from 14.3 cm to 13.1 cm, without evidence of perirenal fluid.

summary.text: A 10-year-old boy with a solitary left kidney and IVC agenesis diagnosed in infancy, superficial abdominal varices since birth, and confirmed compound-heterozygous SERPINC1-related ATIII deficiency presented to the emergency room with severe left-flank pain. Abdominal CT showed left perirenal hematoma with renal infarction, while renal function was normal without proteinuria or hematuria. High-output percutaneous drainage persisted despite warfarin, enoxaparin and ATIII supplementation. Fluid analysis and MR lymphangiography identified non-chylous perirenal lymphatic leakage. The first ethanol sclerotherapy session did not reduce drainage; four sessions over a month reduced the collection and improved symptoms, permitting drain removal and discharge. At six months after discharge he remained stable on warfarin without thromboembolism or hemorrhage and with stable renal function. A comparison ultrasound, whose exact visit timing is not specified, showed less left-kidney enlargement (14.3 to 13.1 cm) and no perirenal fluid. KILT/pseudo-KILT remained a considered classification; introductory and discussion claims conflict about leg thrombosis, so the full triad is not established.
